prompt: What goes wrong if each page view is assigned to a group by a fresh coin flip?

choices.text: The groups come out unequal in size
choices.why: Coin flips give roughly equal groups; the problem is that visitors cross between them.

choices.text: The same visitor ends up in both groups
choices.why: Right. The assignment is random but not sticky.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the coin is fair and the site records every flip in its logs
choices.why: A fair coin per view still puts one person in both versions.

choices.text: It is too slow
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

prompt: Why does the hash include the test's name as well as the visitor's identifier?

choices.text: So that each test shuffles visitors independently
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the same visitors would be treated in every test.

choices.text: To make the hash harder to break, so that visitors cannot choose which version they see
choices.why: Security is not the purpose; independence between tests is.

choices.text: To make the assignment sticky
choices.why: The visitor's identifier alone already does that.

choices.text: Because sha256 needs two inputs
choices.why: It takes one text; the two are joined.

prompt: Panela assigns by cookie. What is one person with a phone and a laptop, to the test?

choices.text: One visitor, since the hash recognises the person behind both devices
choices.why: A hash of a cookie knows nothing about the person.

choices.text: Excluded from the test
choices.why: Nothing excludes them.

choices.text: A cluster
choices.why: A cluster is a unit chosen on purpose, such as a city.

choices.text: Two visitors
choices.why: Right, and possibly in two different groups.

prompt: What p-value did the sample ratio check give for Panela's test, to three decimal places?
A test shows a sample ratio mismatch with p = 0.000004, and the treatment won clearly. What should happen?

choices.text: Ship it; the win is clear
choices.why: With a broken split the win cannot be trusted, however clear.

choices.text: Rebalance the groups by dropping visitors from the larger one, then read the result
choices.why: The missing visitors are not random; dropping more does not bring them back.

choices.text: Do not interpret it; find the fault
choices.why: Right. The cause is in the plumbing.

choices.text: Lower α to compensate
choices.why: α does not fix who was lost.

prompt: The new checkout page crashes on old phones before the visitor is counted. Which way will that bias the test?

choices.text: Against the treatment, since it loses visitors
choices.why: Losing visitors who rarely buy raises the treatment's rate.

choices.text: Towards the treatment
choices.why: Right. It loses exactly the visitors least likely to buy.

choices.text: No bias, because the crash happens at random across the visitors of the new group
choices.why: It happens to old phones, which is not at random.

choices.text: Only the guardrails are affected
choices.why: The primary metric's denominator changes too.

prompt: Why compare the share of mobile visitors between the groups?

choices.text: The treatment cannot change it, so a difference means the groups were built differently
choices.why: Right. It is a check of the randomisation.

choices.text: To see whether the new page works on phones
choices.why: That would compare conversion by device; this compares who arrived.

choices.text: Mobile visitors must be excluded
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson excludes them.

choices.text: It is the primary metric
choices.why: The primary metric is conversion.

prompt: If some visitors see both versions on different devices, what happens to the measured effect?

choices.text: It doubles
choices.why: Mixing makes the groups more alike, not less.

choices.text: It reverses sign, since the control group now holds the visitors most persuaded by the new page
choices.why: Dilution pulls towards zero; a reversal needs much more.

choices.text: Nothing, if the groups stay equal in size
choices.why: Equal sizes say nothing about mixing.

choices.text: It shrinks towards zero
choices.why: Right. Part of each group has seen both.

prompt: Panela tests a new referral page, and friends of treated customers land in both groups. What design avoids that leak?

choices.text: Randomise by page view
choices.why: That breaks stickiness and makes things worse.

choices.text: Double the sample
choices.why: More visitors leak just the same.

choices.text: Randomise clusters, such as cities, that do not talk to each other
choices.why: Right, at a large cost in power.

choices.text: Exclude all referred visitors
choices.why: Then the referral page cannot be tested on the people it is for.

prompt: The treatment raises orders so much that the kitchen delays the control group's boxes. What is wrong with the measured difference?

choices.text: Nothing; more orders are more orders
choices.why: Some of the gap was caused in the control by the test itself.

choices.text: Some of it is a loss inflicted on the other group
choices.why: Right. A shared resource links the groups.

choices.text: It underestimates the effect
choices.why: It overstates it.

choices.text: The sample ratio is broken
choices.why: Group sizes can be perfect here.

prompt: In week 1 the new checkout converted 5.35% and the old 4.31%. What was the lift, in percentage points?

choices.text: A lift that fades as visitors get used to the change
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A higher conversion among visitors who are new to the site, whatever version they see
choices.why: That is a difference between kinds of visitor, not a reaction to change.

choices.text: The first week of any test
choices.why: A first week can be normal; the effect is the fading.

choices.text: A drop for returning visitors
choices.why: That is change aversion, its mirror.

prompt: The test's three-week average lift is driven by week 1. What happens if the change is shipped on the strength of that average?

choices.text: It delivers the average, since the average already weighs every week of the test equally
choices.why: Equal weights still include a week that will not recur.

choices.text: It delivers more, as novelty spreads
choices.why: Novelty fades; it does not spread.

choices.text: Nothing can be said
choices.why: The weekly lifts say a good deal.

choices.text: It delivers less than promised
choices.why: Right. Everyone after launch is past their first week.

prompt: Why does splitting new and returning visitors help diagnose a novelty effect?

choices.text: New visitors are excluded from A/B tests
choices.why: Panela's checkout test is entirely about them.

choices.text: Returning visitors never convert
choices.why: They do, often more.

choices.text: Novelty hits those who knew the old design
choices.why: Right. A first-time visitor has nothing to be surprised by.

choices.text: It doubles the sample size, since each visitor is then counted once in each of the two subgroups
choices.why: Splitting divides a sample; it never doubles it.
